items.bodyEn: Every post town kept a honjin, the official lodging where daimyō and court nobles slept on their journeys. More than a hundred stood along the Tōkaidō; only two buildings survive, at Kusatsu and here at Futagawa. The Futagawa honjin, kept by the Baba family through the last decades of the Edo period, is now a museum of the road.
items.sourceNote: Futagawa-juku Honjin Museum records (Toyohashi); Tōkaidō post-town surveys

items.bodyEn: Hiroshige's Futagawa print shows Saru-ga-Baba, a lonely moor of low pines, crossed by three goze — blind women who traveled in small troupes, singing to the shamisen for lodging and coins, a profession recorded since medieval times. They head for a teahouse whose sign reads 名物かしわ餅: kashiwa-mochi, rice cakes wrapped in oak leaves, the local specialty.
items.ja: {名物|めいぶつ}かしわ{餅|もち}

items.titleEn: Shade and Deeds: おかげ and せい
items.bodyEn: 〜おかげで credits, 〜せいで blames, but both began as plain nouns. お陰 is the honorable 'shade': shelter under a god's or Buddha's protection, which is why おかげさまで thanks an unseen favor. せい is a worn-down 所為 (しょい), 'what was done', the cause. Today せい has gone sour, so 〜おかげで after a bad result reads as sarcasm.
items.sourceNote: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten / Kōjien, entries おかげ (御陰) and せい (所為)

items.bodyEn: 'Kindness is not for other people's sake' — it circles back to you, so be kind. Many Japanese now read it as 'kindness does people no good', because ならず, the classical 'is not' built on the ず of Arai, gets mistaken for 'does not become'. 為 is the formal 'for the sake of' behind this station's 〜ため(に).
items.ja: {情|なさ}けは{人|ひと}の{為|ため}ならず
items.kana: なさけはひとのためならず
